non_convex_optimization.summary: Restarts a local descent from many random points and hops between basins of the trading-utility surface, keeping the basin whose rule holds up on validation.
non_convex_optimization.implementationNote: Bridge: the optimiser is the model's trainer; it searches a tanh-linear position rule against train-span net utility on the price tape (next-open fills, round-trip cost); validation picks the generation kept; P(up) is a logistic curve of w.x+b fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: scipy basin hopping over L-BFGS-B descents, one restart per epoch. Expect: an in-sample-optimised linear rule, edge near the base rate.
non_convex_optimization.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

epochs.description: How many random restarts (one engine epoch each).

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

hop_count.label: Hops per restart
hop_count.description: Perturb-then-descend steps of basin hopping in each restart.

temperature.label: Acceptance temperature
temperature.description: Metropolis temperature: a worse basin is accepted with probability exp(-increase / T).

perturbation_scale.label: Hop size
perturbation_scale.description: Size of the random jump between basins (weight units).

local_iteration_limit.label: Local descent iterations
local_iteration_limit.description: At most this many L-BFGS-B iterations per local descent.

weight_decay.label: Ridge penalty on the weights
weight_decay.description: Subtracted from the training utility per unit of squared weight; larger keeps the rule simpler.

weight_bound.label: Weight bound
weight_bound.description: Every weight and the bias are searched inside [-bound, bound] (features are z-scores).

native.produces: The best decision vector found within a search budget of restarts or perturbation jumps, its objective value, and no proof that it is the global best.
native.targetVariable: The parameter vector that gives the lowest value found of a multi-modal objective; it is a statement about the objective surface that was searched, not about the next price move.
native.objectiveNote: The method is a global strategy wrapped around a local descent, here random restarts with basin-hopping jumps accepted by a Metropolis rule, and it applies to any objective handed to it; the tape utility is the objective the Model Cycle gives it.

metrics.why: With no stopping rule except the restart budget, the curve of the lowest objective found against restarts spent is how the specification itself says to judge the search: it has done its job when further restarts stop improving it.
metrics.baseline: The objective value of the first restart's local optimum.

metrics.why: A deep basin found on one span can be a pit dug by noise, so the kept point's own objective on bars that neither the restarts nor the choice of basin ever touched is the test of whether the basin is real.
metrics.baseline: The same kept point's mean utility per decision on its own training tape.

metrics.why: The specification names the share of restarts that descend into the same basin as the best one as its only confidence signal, a heuristic and never a proof of global optimality.
Every restart and every hop is another draw from the objective surface, so the count of points evaluated states how much luck could sit inside the best value found.
Random starting points and random perturbations mean a new seed can settle in a different basin, so the spread of the result across seeds is the honest error bar of a method with no certificate.
When a held-back span chooses which restart's basin is kept, the winning value is the maximum over restarts and so flatters the kept point; it is shown only beside the untouched test value.
metrics.baseline: The kept point's objective on the test span.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: It measures a trading rule and its costs, which exist only once the Model Cycle trades the kept position rule; natively the search is graded by the objective it found.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no return stream exist in a restart search, and the metric registry carries no alpha measure.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It describes an equity path over many bars, while the native result is a single best-found parameter vector.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover is at most a cost term inside the searched objective and never a measure of the search itself.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It needs annualised profit and a drawdown, neither of which exists before the best-found point is traded.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: Tail risk can be the multi-modal objective being searched, yet it does not tell whether the restarts reached a good basin.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: No dual bound exists for a multi-modal objective, so there is no proven distance between the best basin found and the global best.

asRun.standInNote: The search is the specification's basin hopping with a limited-memory quasi-Newton local descent and one restart per epoch, but it is applied to one fixed problem: the weights of a hyperbolic-tangent linear position rule scored by net utility on the training reward tape; validation tape utility picks the restart kept and a logistic curve fitted on validation bars turns the rule's score into the probability of up, so the as-run numbers measure that kept rule plus that curve. The market does not react to the rule and its position is not part of its input.
asRun.probabilityNote: The kept restart's linear score of the bar's feature row is passed through a logistic curve whose slope and intercept are fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars; the search itself maximised utility, so the raw score has no probability meaning before the curve.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the mean net utility per decision bar in move-scale units; the training value also carries the ridge penalty and the validation value does not

meaningful.why: The restarts searched for the position rule that made the most money on the training tape after costs, so the profit of its call on the test walk is the closest out-of-sample reading of what it was optimised for, on bars that neither the search nor the choice of restart touched.
The logistic curve is monotone, so the ordering of bars is the kept rule's own score and this number tests whether a rule tuned for tape utility also ranks up bars above down bars.
Holding the same series long is the reference that shows whether the basin the search settled in learned anything beyond the drift of the training span.
It tests how steady the per-bar profit of the kept rule's call is under the engine's rule; the search maximised mean utility with no charge for variability.
The tape utility being searched has no drawdown term, so the deepest fall of the traded equity shows a risk the optimiser was never asked to control.
It compares winning and losing trades made by flips of the kept rule's call, while the search itself was paid per decision bar and not per closed trade.
It counts trades that closed in profit after costs, which depends on the engine's exits as well as on the rule's sign.
It grades the stated odds of the kept rule's score after the validation-fitted curve; the rule was selected on validation tape utility and not on this loss, so on test bars it is a fair second view.
A bounded view of the same rule-plus-curve probability, which matters because a utility-trained score with little directional content is mapped close to one half.
It checks whether the curve fitted on validation bars still maps the rule's score to the right frequencies on test bars; few bins are filled when the curve is flat.
It scores the cut of the curve at one half, which is the traded call and depends on the validation-fitted intercept as well as on the searched weights.
It shows whether the kept rule's call finds both up and down bars or sits on the side that paid on the training tape.
One symmetric number for the rule-plus-curve call, near zero when the basin found amounts to a constant long or short lean.
The forecast comes from a second linear model that the same basin-hopping search fitted to the scaled move with a Huber loss, so this tests that second search against forecasting no move.
It is the miss in points of the separately searched Huber-fitted forecast, read against the no-change error on the same bars.
It is the sign accuracy of the second, Huber-fitted model and so can disagree with the traded call, which comes from the utility-searched rule.
Each epoch is one restart, so the training loss by epoch is the local optimum each restart reached and shows whether more restarts were still finding deeper basins.
It is the validation tape utility of the restart that was kept, the maximum over restarts and therefore optimistic; it is read only beside the test profit.
The count of objective evaluations over all hops and descents states how many points of the utility surface were tried before one was kept.
The searched utility charges one round trip per decision bar, while the engine charges only when the call flips, so the turnover shows how far the two cost models differ for this rule.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training value includes the ridge penalty and comes from a different tape than the validation value, and the validation value was the selection score.
With long only off and no stop or target the engine is always in the market, so the share describes the engine's rule; the rule's own fractional position size is overridden.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, so it is not a same-model reference for the rule-plus-curve probability.

caveats: The engine trades the sign of the curve's output at full size, so the fractional position the hyperbolic-tangent rule was optimised with, and its implied preference for staying small, are overridden.
The validation loss by epoch is minus the validation tape utility and not a logarithmic loss, and it is the number that chose the kept restart.
The logistic curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the same validation bars that chose the restart, so only the test walk is out of sample for the probability.
Moves on the training tape are clipped before the search so one extreme bar cannot own the utility, which the test walk does not do.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so any interval on these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For any root other than the micro Nasdaq contract the costs charged are that contract's account figures applied as a stated assumption, and the last bar of each fold exits at its close.

differential_evolution.summary: Evolves a population of trading rules by adding scaled differences of members to each other and keeping a child only when it trades better.
differential_evolution.implementationNote: Bridge: the optimiser is the model's trainer; it searches a tanh-linear position rule against train-span net utility on the price tape (next-open fills, round-trip cost); validation picks the generation kept; P(up) is a logistic curve of w.x+b fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: scipy's DE/rand/1/bin, one generation per epoch. Expect: an in-sample-optimised linear rule, edge near the base rate.
differential_evolution.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

epochs.label: Generations
epochs.description: How many generations the search runs (one engine epoch each).

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

mutation_scale.label: Mutation scale (F)
mutation_scale.description: How far a difference vector moves the mutant.

crossover_probability.label: Crossover probability
crossover_probability.description: Chance each coordinate is taken from the mutant.

weight_decay.label: Ridge penalty on the weights
weight_decay.description: Subtracted from the training utility per unit of squared weight; larger keeps the rule simpler.

weight_bound.label: Weight bound
weight_bound.description: Every weight and the bias are searched inside [-bound, bound] (features are z-scores).

native.produces: The best parameter vector its population found for a score that can only be evaluated and never differentiated, together with that score and the final spread of the population, with no proof that a better vector does not exist.
native.targetVariable: The value of the black-box score the search is pointed at for one candidate parameter vector, which on this dashboard is the net utility after costs of a position rule on the reward tape of the training bars.
native.objectiveNote: Differential evolution carries no objective of its own: it improves whatever score it is handed by building each trial vector from the scaled difference of two population members added to a third and keeping the trial only when it scores at least as well, and the tape utility is the score this dashboard hands it.

metrics.why: A trial vector replaces its target only when it scores at least as well, so the best score in the population can hold or improve but never fall, and drawing it against the count of scored candidates shows how many generations of that one-for-one replacement the answer really cost.
metrics.baseline: The best score in the starting population of the same run, before any difference-vector mutation has happened.

metrics.why: Every generation scores the population on the same stretch of history, so the net utility per decision of the kept vector on later bars, where no trial was ever scored and no generation was picked, is the only reading that separates real structure from a vector fitted to that one stretch.
metrics.baseline: The same kept vector's net utility per decision on the training tape it was searched on, and the zero utility of staying flat on the same test tape.

metrics.why: The population size multiplied by the generations run is the number of parameter vectors scored against one history, and the more trial vectors the greedy replacement has sifted through, the larger the share of the winning score that is the luck of the draw.

The starting population and the choice of which three members build each mutant are random, so two runs end on different vectors, and the spread of their later-bar utility shows whether a result belongs to the method or to one draw of the dice.

When a later validation stretch decides which generation's best vector is kept, the utility on that stretch is the highest of many looks and therefore flatters the vector, so it is shown only beside the value on bars nothing was chosen on.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: It grades the rule and costs the population was scored on and not the search, so natively it never applied; the as-run layer reports the engine's Sharpe ratio of the kept rule's calls.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no beta are fitted anywhere in the method or the engine, so an alpha figure was never something this optimiser could produce.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a property of the traded equity path under the engine's rule, reported as run, and carries no information about the quality of the difference-vector search.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The method tunes one vector of parameters and holds no portfolio; the nearest real quantity is the as-run count of trades per session day.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It divides the engine's return by the engine's drawdown, both as-run quantities of the traded rule and neither a native output of the population.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The search returns a parameter vector and its score and never a distribution of losses, and the registry holds no tail-loss metric to map this row to.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: The population gives a best vector found so far and never a proven bound on the best possible score, so there is no gap to a certified optimum to report.

notApplicable.name: Gradient norm
notApplicable.why: The method never computes a slope of the score, it only compares a trial vector with its target, so there is no gradient whose size could be watched.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: Natively the search returns a parameter vector and a score and states no probability of an up move, so a score for stated odds has nothing to grade until the as-run bridge adds a fitted curve.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model uses the specified optimiser, differential evolution with a random base member, one difference vector and binomial crossover from the scipy library, but it is pointed at one fixed job: finding the weights of a linear position rule, whose position is the hyperbolic tangent of a weighted sum of the bar's features, that maximise net utility after costs on the training reward tape. The probability of up is then a logistic curve of that weighted sum fitted on the validation bars, so the as-run numbers measure an in-sample-optimised linear rule plus that curve and not the optimiser in general.
asRun.probabilityNote: The kept rule gives each bar a weighted sum of its features, and the probability of up is a logistic curve of that sum whose slope and intercept are fitted by maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only, with no class weighting.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the mean net utility per bar in move-scale units; the training value belongs to the best vector found so far and adds the ridge penalty, the validation value is the same vector on the validation tape with no penalty

meaningful.why: The population was evolved to maximise net utility after costs on the training tape, so the money the kept rule's calls made on the test bars is the as-run number closest to its own objective, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.
It shows how steadily the kept linear rule earned per bar after costs on bars the difference-vector search never scored, which tells a repeatable edge from a rule fitted to the training tape.
A rule searched on a rising training tape can end up long nearly always, and subtracting buy and hold on the same folds shows whether the evolved weights added anything to simply holding.

The training utility is an average over bars that pays each decision as a separate trade and never sees a string of losses, so the deepest hole in the traded equity is a risk the population was not scored on.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the trades the kept rule's side changes produced, after costs, and is read with the trade count because a rule with small weights rarely changes side.

It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the kept rule's call flips, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it describes the engine's rule applied to this rule's calls.
The search charges one round trip per decision on the tape, while the engine charges only when the call flips, and this turnover shows how often the kept rule actually changed side.
It counts how often the curve of the weighted sum crossed one half or a trade otherwise ended, which every trading number of this rule has to be read with.
It shows how often the kept rule called up, which exposes a population that converged on a bias term and calls one side through the whole test span.

The rule was searched for utility and not for hit rate, so the share of bars where the curve of its weighted sum landed on the right side of one half tests whether money-seeking weights also point the right way, beside the majority-class accuracy of the same fold.
Averaging the hit rate on up bars and on down bars gives no credit to a kept rule that leans one way on every bar, which a utility search on a trending tape readily produces.
It sums up the four cells of the kept rule's hard calls in one symmetric number that stays near zero when the evolved weights carry nothing beyond a fixed lean.

The weighted sum is continuous and the fitted curve only rescales it, so this tests whether bars the kept rule scored higher went up more often, with the reminder that a negative fitted slope reverses the order.
It grades the logistic curve of the weighted sum as a squared miss, which is a fair bounded score for the rule plus its curve, whose two parameters were fitted on validation bars.
The optimiser never aimed at stated odds, so this number grades the validation-fitted curve laid over the evolved weighted sum and shows whether that curve still holds on the test bars.

It checks whether the chances quoted by the validation-fitted curve matched the observed up share on test bars, read with the occupied-bin count because a weak rule keeps the curve close to even odds.
A slope away from one on the test bars means the curve fitted on the short validation span no longer matches how the evolved weighted sum relates to outcomes.

The price line is a second population evolved by the same optimiser on the Huber loss of a linear forecast of the scaled move, so this tests differential evolution as a regression fitter against forecasting no move and says nothing about the traded rule.
It is the typical miss in points of that second, separately evolved linear forecast after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's miss on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the second evolved forecast matched the actual move where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it belongs to different weights from the traded rule and can disagree with its call.
The fit summary records how many weight vectors the population scored on the training tape, and the kept rule's in-sample utility is the best of that many tries.

It is the selection score that chose population_size, mutation_scale, crossover_probability, weight_decay and weight_bound on training blocks, a second layer of picking on top of the evolution and flattered by it.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Neither the utility search nor the validation curve weights the classes, so a score that gives each class half the weight grades the rule against a target it never aimed at.

The training value is the best vector's utility with the ridge penalty added and the validation value has no penalty and is the number the kept generation was picked on, so their difference is not a clean overfit reading.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short after the first call, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the evolved weights.

caveats: The generation kept is the one whose best vector had the highest net utility on the validation tape, so every validation figure is optimistic and only the test walk is out of sample.

The traded side is the fitted curve of the weighted sum compared with one half, and because that curve has its own intercept and a slope that may be negative, the side traded can differ from the sign of the position the search optimised.

The search scores a position between minus one and one and pays one round trip on every bar's decision, while the engine trades a fixed size by the side of the call and pays costs only when the call flips, so the test numbers are not the training utility measured on new bars.
The vector reported each epoch is the best in-sample vector found so far, so choosing an epoch on validation chooses when to stop a sequence that only improves on the training tape.

The price line comes from a second differential evolution run on the Huber loss of the scaled move, kept on validation Huber loss, so forecast metrics and direction metrics grade two different weight vectors.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short after the first call, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the sampled weights.

caveats: The generation kept is the one whose best-so-far sample had the highest net utility on the validation tape, so every validation figure is optimistic and only the test walk is out of sample.
The rule kept is the single best sample ever drawn and not the mean of the search distribution, so it carries the upward luck of a best-of-many draw that the mean would not.

The traded side is the fitted curve of the weighted sum compared with one half, and because that curve has its own intercept and a slope that may be negative, the side traded can differ from the sign of the position the search optimised.

The search scores a position between minus one and one and pays one round trip on every bar's decision, while the engine trades a fixed size by the side of the call and pays costs only when the call flips, so the test numbers are not the training utility measured on new bars.

The price line comes from a second covariance matrix adaptation run on the Huber loss of the scaled move, kept on validation Huber loss, so forecast metrics and direction metrics grade two different weight vectors.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

genetic_algorithm.summary: Breeds trading rules whose genes say which features to use and how much; the fitter rules reproduce, cross and mutate each generation.
genetic_algorithm.implementationNote: Bridge: the optimiser is the model's trainer; it searches a tanh-linear position rule against train-span net utility on the price tape (next-open fills, round-trip cost); validation picks the generation kept; P(up) is a logistic curve of w.x+b fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: chromosome = feature-inclusion bits plus weights (DEAP). Expect: an in-sample-optimised linear rule, edge near the base rate.
genetic_algorithm.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

epochs.label: Generations
epochs.description: How many generations the search runs (one engine epoch each).

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

crossover_probability.label: Crossover probability
crossover_probability.description: Chance a pair of parents is crossed.

mutation_probability.label: Mutation probability per gene
mutation_probability.description: Chance each gene is flipped or perturbed.

tournament_size.label: Tournament size
tournament_size.description: Candidates compared to pick each parent; larger is greedier.

elite_count.label: Elite carried over
elite_count.description: The best rules copied unchanged into the next generation.

feature_penalty.label: Penalty per included feature
feature_penalty.description: Subtracted from the utility for each feature the rule uses.

weight_decay.label: Ridge penalty on the weights
weight_decay.description: Subtracted from the training utility per unit of squared weight; larger keeps the rule simpler.

weight_bound.label: Weight bound
weight_bound.description: Every weight and the bias are searched inside [-bound, bound] (features are z-scores).

native.produces: The fittest chromosome its population bred, decoded into which rule parts or features are switched on and what their values are, together with its fitness and the final diversity of the population, with no proof that a fitter chromosome does not exist.
native.targetVariable: The fitness of one chromosome, which on this dashboard is the net utility after costs of the position rule the chromosome encodes on the reward tape of the training bars.
native.objectiveNote: A genetic algorithm has no objective of its own: tournament selection, crossover of two parents and mutation of single genes improve whatever fitness function they are given, and because the chromosome can carry on and off genes the search also decides which features the rule uses; the tape utility is the fitness this dashboard supplies.

metrics.why: With the elite chromosomes carried forward unchanged the best fitness never drops, so drawing it against the count of chromosomes scored shows whether crossover was still joining useful building blocks or the population had collapsed early onto one mediocre chromosome.
metrics.baseline: The best fitness in the random starting population of the same run, before any selection, crossover or mutation.

metrics.why: Selection breeds from whatever scored well on one stretch of history, and a population will exploit a quirk of that stretch as eagerly as a real pattern, so the fittest chromosome's net utility per decision on later bars it was neither bred nor chosen on is the reading that matters.
metrics.baseline: The same chromosome's net utility per decision on the training tape it was bred on, and the zero utility of staying flat on the same test tape.

metrics.why: The population size multiplied by the generations is the number of chromosomes scored on the same history, and with on and off genes multiplying the combinations, the fittest of that many looks good partly by chance.

The chromosome's on and off genes say which features the rule reads, so if the switched-on set changes from one training span to the next the population found a coincidence of one span and not a rule worth naming.

The starting chromosomes, the tournament draws, the crossover points and the mutated genes are all random, so a new seed breeds a different winner, and the spread of later-bar utility over seeds shows how much of a result is that randomness.

When a later validation stretch decides which generation's fittest chromosome is kept, the utility on that stretch is the top of many looks and reads too well, so it is displayed only beside the value on bars no choice was made on.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: It grades the rule and costs used as the fitness function and not the breeding, so natively it never applied; the as-run layer reports the engine's Sharpe ratio of the kept rule's calls.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no beta are fitted by the genetic search or by the engine, so an alpha was never a quantity this optimiser could output.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a property of the traded equity path under the engine's rule, reported as run, and tells nothing about whether the population bred a good chromosome.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The algorithm evolves one chromosome and holds no portfolio; the nearest real quantity is the as-run count of trades per session day.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It is the engine's return divided by the engine's drawdown, both as-run quantities of the traded rule and neither produced by the genetic operators.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The algorithm returns a chromosome and its fitness and never a distribution of losses, and the registry has no tail-loss metric for this row.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: Breeding gives a fittest chromosome found so far and never a proven bound on the best possible fitness, so there is no certified gap to report.

notApplicable.name: Gradient norm
notApplicable.why: Selection, crossover and mutation never compute a slope of the fitness, and on and off genes have none, so there is no gradient to measure.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: Natively the algorithm returns a chromosome and its fitness and states no probability of an up move, so a probability score has nothing to grade until the as-run bridge adds a fitted curve.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model uses the specified operators from the deap library, tournament selection, crossover, per-gene mutation and elite chromosomes carried forward, but on one fixed chromosome: an on or off gene and a weight for every feature plus a bias, decoded into a linear position rule whose position is the hyperbolic tangent of the weighted sum of the switched-on features. Fitness is net utility after costs on the training reward tape less a ridge penalty and a charge per switched-on feature, and the probability of up is a logistic curve of the weighted sum fitted on the validation bars, so the as-run numbers measure an in-sample-bred linear rule plus that curve and not a search over discrete trading rules in general.
asRun.probabilityNote: The kept chromosome gives each bar a weighted sum of its switched-on features, and the probability of up is a logistic curve of that sum whose slope and intercept are fitted by maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only, with no class weighting.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the mean net utility per bar in move-scale units; the training value belongs to the fittest chromosome found so far and adds the ridge penalty and the charge per switched-on feature, the validation value is the same chromosome on the validation tape with neither

meaningful.why: The chromosomes were bred for net utility after costs on the training tape, so the money the kept chromosome's calls made on the test bars is the as-run number closest to its own fitness, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.

It shows how steadily the kept chromosome's rule earned per bar after costs on bars no chromosome was ever scored on, which tells a repeatable edge from a feature set and weights bred to fit the training tape.

Breeding on a rising training tape can favour chromosomes that are long nearly always, and subtracting buy and hold on the same folds shows whether the chosen features and weights added anything to simply holding.
Fitness is an average utility that pays each decision as a separate trade and never sees losses in a row, so the deepest hole in the traded equity is a risk no chromosome was selected on.

It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the trades the kept chromosome's side changes produced, after costs, and is read with the trade count because a chromosome with few features switched on rarely changes side.

It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the kept chromosome's call flips, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it describes the engine's rule applied to this rule's calls.
Fitness charges one round trip per decision on the tape, while the engine charges only when the call flips, and this turnover shows how often the kept chromosome's rule actually changed side.
It counts how often the curve of the weighted sum crossed one half or a trade otherwise ended, which every trading number of this bred rule has to be read with.
It shows how often the kept chromosome called up, which exposes a population that switched nearly every feature off and left the bias gene to call one side through the test span.

The chromosomes were bred for utility and not for hit rate, so the share of bars where the curve of the weighted sum landed on the right side of one half tests whether money-seeking genes also point the right way, beside the majority-class accuracy of the same fold.
Averaging the hit rate on up bars and on down bars gives no credit to a kept chromosome that leans one way on every bar, which breeding for utility on a trending tape readily produces.
It sums up the four cells of the kept chromosome's hard calls in one symmetric number that stays near zero when the surviving genes carry nothing beyond a fixed lean.

The weighted sum of the switched-on features is continuous and the fitted curve only rescales it, so this tests whether bars the chromosome scored higher went up more often, with the reminder that a negative fitted slope reverses the order.
It grades the logistic curve of the chromosome's weighted sum as a squared miss, which is a fair bounded score for the rule plus its curve, whose two parameters were fitted on validation bars.

Selection, crossover and mutation never aimed at stated odds, so this number grades the validation-fitted curve laid over the bred weighted sum and shows whether that curve still holds on the test bars.

It checks whether the chances quoted by the validation-fitted curve matched the observed up share on test bars, read with the occupied-bin count because a chromosome with few live genes keeps the curve close to even odds.
A slope away from one on the test bars means the curve fitted on the short validation span no longer matches how the bred weighted sum relates to outcomes.

The price line is a second population bred by the same operators on the Huber loss of a linear forecast of the scaled move, so this tests the genetic algorithm as a regression fitter against forecasting no move and says nothing about the traded rule.
It is the typical miss in points of that second, separately bred linear forecast after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's miss on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the second bred forecast matched the actual move where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it belongs to a different chromosome from the traded rule and can disagree with its call.

The fit summary records how many chromosomes were scored on the training tape, and with an on or off gene per feature the kept rule's in-sample utility is the best of that many feature sets and weightings.

It is the selection score that chose population_size, crossover_probability, mutation_probability and tournament_size on training blocks, a second layer of picking on top of the breeding and flattered by it.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Neither the utility fitness nor the validation curve weights the classes, so a score that gives each class half the weight grades the rule against a target it never aimed at.

The training value is the fittest chromosome's utility with the ridge penalty and the feature charge added and the validation value has neither and is the number the kept generation was picked on, so their difference is not a clean overfit reading.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short after the first call, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the bred chromosome.

caveats: The generation kept is the one whose fittest-so-far chromosome had the highest net utility on the validation tape, so every validation figure is optimistic and only the test walk is out of sample.

The traded side is the fitted curve of the weighted sum compared with one half, and because that curve has its own intercept and a slope that may be negative, the side traded can differ from the sign of the position the chromosome was bred for.

Fitness scores a position between minus one and one and pays one round trip on every bar's decision, while the engine trades a fixed size by the side of the call and pays costs only when the call flips, so the test numbers are not the training fitness measured on new bars.
The set of switched-on features is chosen on the training span alone and is refitted on every fold, so a feature kept in one fold may be switched off in the next.
The price line comes from a second genetic run on the Huber loss of the scaled move, kept on validation Huber loss, so forecast metrics and direction metrics grade two different chromosomes.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

gradient_descent.summary: Walks the weights of a logistic model downhill on the whole training span at every step, with momentum, and stops where validation is best.
gradient_descent.implementationNote: Bridge: full-batch gradient descent with heavy-ball momentum on the log loss (plus ridge) of a linear model; P(up) is its own sigmoid(w.x+b), and validation log loss picks the stopping epoch. Differs from the spec: none beyond the fixed model (a logistic regression) that makes the optimiser visible. Expect: close to the logistic regression entry; that is the point of comparison.
gradient_descent.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

epochs.label: Epochs
epochs.description: Epochs of iterations_per_epoch full-batch steps each.

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

learning_rate.label: Learning rate
learning_rate.description: Step size of each gradient step.

momentum.label: Momentum
momentum.description: Share of the previous step carried into the next (heavy ball).

learning_rate_decay.label: Learning-rate decay per step
learning_rate_decay.description: The learning rate is multiplied by this after every step.

iterations_per_epoch.label: Steps per epoch
iterations_per_epoch.description: Full-batch gradient steps between two validation checks.

weight_decay.label: Ridge penalty on the weights
weight_decay.description: Subtracted from the training utility per unit of squared weight; larger keeps the rule simpler.

native.produces: The parameter vector reached by stepping again and again against the slope of a smooth loss computed over the whole training set, together with the final loss and the size of the gradient where it stopped, with no certificate beyond that gradient size.
native.targetVariable: The value of the smooth loss at the current parameters, which on this dashboard is the logarithmic loss of a linear model's probability that the close label horizon bars ahead finishes above this bar's close.
native.objectiveNote: Gradient descent is an update rule and not a model, so it minimises whichever differentiable loss it is given; the logarithmic loss of a linear model with a penalty on the size of the weights is the loss fixed on this dashboard so that the walk downhill can be watched, and momentum carries part of each step into the next.

metrics.why: Each step uses the exact slope over the whole training set, so the loss against the count of steps is the method's own product: it shows whether the learning rate let the weights slide to the bottom, crawl, or bounce from side to side of the valley.
metrics.baseline: The loss at the starting weights of the same run, before the first step downhill.

metrics.why: The steps drive down the logarithmic loss on the training rows, so the same quantity on later rows the walk never touched says whether the point it stopped at states honest odds or only sits low on the training surface.
metrics.baseline: The logarithmic loss of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar.

metrics.why: Stopping the walk before the bottom and penalising large weights both leave the weighted sum shorter than a full fit would make it, and this slope shows whether the resulting log-odds are squeezed toward even or stretched too far.
metrics.baseline: A slope of one, the mathematical value for log-odds on the right scale.

metrics.why: The walk has arrived only where the slope is flat, so the size of the full-batch gradient at the last step is the method's own stopping evidence, and a large value means the weights were still moving when the budget ran out.

Reading the training loss and the later-row loss side by side at every checkpoint shows the moment the downhill walk on the training surface stops helping on unseen rows, which is where the steps should end.

When both numbers are the plain logarithmic loss of the weights reached, their difference at the stopping point shows how far the walk had started fitting the training rows themselves, which more steps and a weaker weight penalty both enlarge.
metrics.baseline: Zero, meaning the weights score the same on rows they were stepped on and rows they never saw.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The update rule minimises a smooth loss and takes no position, so natively this never applied; the as-run layer reports the engine's Sharpe ratio of the fitted model's calls.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no beta are fitted by the descent or by the engine, so an alpha was never a quantity this optimiser could output.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a property of the traded equity path under the engine's rule, reported as run, and tells nothing about whether the steps reached the bottom of the loss.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The method fits one weight vector and holds no portfolio; the nearest real quantity is the as-run count of trades per session day.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It is the engine's return divided by the engine's drawdown, both as-run quantities of the traded calls and neither produced by stepping against a gradient.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The descent returns weights, a loss and a gradient size and never a distribution of trading losses, and the registry has no tail-loss metric for this row.

notApplicable.name: Return dispersion across seeds
notApplicable.why: A full-batch walk from fixed starting weights uses no random draw, so every seed gives the same weights and there is no spread across seeds to report.

notApplicable.name: Mean test-tape return of the policy's own action
notApplicable.why: The loss being walked down is a logarithmic loss on labels and not a utility on a reward tape, so this member of the optimiser family has no tape return of its own.

notApplicable.name: Candidate evaluation count
notApplicable.why: The walk follows one path of weights and never compares a population of rivals, so there is no best-of-many pick whose luck would need counting.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: The method reports the gradient size where it stopped and computes no proven bound on the lowest reachable loss, so no certified gap exists.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model uses the specified optimiser, full-batch gradient descent with heavy-ball momentum, but it is pointed at one fixed job: the unweighted logarithmic loss plus a ridge penalty of a linear model of the bar's features, so the model being fitted is a logistic regression made fixed in order to make the optimiser visible. The stopping epoch is chosen on validation logarithmic loss and patience and not by the gradient-size tolerance the specification lists, so the as-run numbers describe that fixed linear classifier and not gradient descent in general.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the sigmoid of the weighted sum of the bar's features under the weights reached by full-batch gradient descent with momentum on the unweighted logarithmic loss plus a ridge penalty, with no curve fitted on top.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per bar; the training value adds the ridge penalty on the weights and the validation value does not

meaningful.why: The full-batch steps walked the weights downhill on unweighted logarithmic loss, so on the test walk this is the descent's own objective measured where neither the steps nor the choice of stopping epoch ever saw the bars.

The weighted sum is continuous, so this tests whether bars the descended weights scored higher went up more often over the label horizon, whatever early stopping and the ridge penalty did to the size of the weights.
It grades the sigmoid of the weighted sum as a squared miss, a bounded second opinion on the same odds that a few bars with extreme feature values cannot dominate.

Because the loss is unweighted, the sigmoid output is a real frequency claim against the base rate, and the binned gap shows whether a stated chance of up matched the observed up share; it is read with the occupied-bin count because an early-stopped walk from zero weights keeps its odds close to even.
It shows without bins whether stopping the walk at the best validation epoch and penalising the weights left the log-odds too flat or too steep on the test bars.
The walk starts at zero weights where every bar gets even odds, and this spread shows how far the steps taken before stopping moved the sigmoid output away from that flat start.

It is the share of scored bars where the sigmoid landed on the right side of one half, and because the loss is unweighted that cut carries the training base rate, so it is read beside the majority-class accuracy of the same fold.
It shows whether the descended weights added anything to the bias term, which alone would call the fold's training majority direction on every bar.
It averages how often the fitted weights caught the up bars and how often the down bars, so a walk that mostly moved the bias and calls one side nearly always earns no credit.
It sums up the four cells of the fitted model's hard calls in one symmetric number that stays near zero when the weighted sum only echoes the training base rate.

It is what the side of the sigmoid's call earned after costs under the engine's rule of following the latest call and filling at the next bar's open, read beside buy and hold on the same folds; the descent itself never saw prices or costs.

It is the per-bar reward for risk of trading the fitted model's call under the engine's rule and costs, and it depends only on which side of one half the sigmoid fell, never on how low the loss was driven.
It is the deepest fall of the equity made by trading the fitted model's call, which shows what one fixed set of descended weights costs when the test bars stop behaving like the training span.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the closed trades the fitted model's side changes produced, after costs, as a description of the engine's rule applied to this model's calls.
It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the sigmoid crosses one half, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it is read with the trade count.
It shows how often the fitted model called up, which exposes a short walk whose bias term decides nearly every bar.
It counts how often the sigmoid crossed one half or a trade otherwise ended, which is needed to read every trading number of a model whose weighted sum stays near zero.

It grades a second linear model fitted by the same full-batch descent on the Huber loss of the scaled move against forecasting no move on the same resolved bars; it says nothing about the classifier's odds.
It is the typical miss in points of that separately descended forecast line after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's miss on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the forecast line matched the actual move on bars where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it belongs to the second set of weights and can disagree with the traded call.
It is the selection score that chose learning_rate, momentum and weight_decay on training blocks, optimistic because it was picked on, and shown only beside the test value.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The descent minimises an unweighted loss, so its odds are centred on the training base rate and a score that gives each class half the weight would grade it against a target it never aimed at.
The training curve holds the logarithmic loss plus the ridge penalty on the weights and the validation curve holds the plain logarithmic loss, so their difference mixes the penalty with any overfit.

The searcher keeps the size of the full-batch gradient in its own search statistics but does not report it through the engine's per-step channel, so the engine's gradient-norm series is empty for this model.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short after the first call, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the descended weights.

caveats: The kept epoch is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, so the validation figure is optimistic and only the test walk is out of sample.
Stopping is decided by validation loss and patience and not by the gradient-size tolerance the specification lists, so the weights kept are usually short of the bottom of the training loss.

The price line is a second model, the same descent run on the Huber loss of the scaled move and kept on validation Huber loss, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade two different sets of weights.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

ant_colony_optimization.summary: Ants sample new trading rules around an archive of the best ones found so far; the archive is the pheromone, and poor rules fade out of it.
ant_colony_optimization.implementationNote: Bridge: the optimiser is the model's trainer; it searches a tanh-linear position rule against train-span net utility on the price tape (next-open fills, round-trip cost); validation picks the generation kept; P(up) is a logistic curve of w.x+b fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: continuous ACO_R, since graph routing has no per-bar meaning. Expect: an in-sample-optimised linear rule, edge near the base rate.
ant_colony_optimization.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

archive_size.label: Archive size (pheromone)
archive_size.description: How many of the best rules the colony remembers.

locality.label: Locality (q)
locality.description: Small values make the ants follow the very best rules.

deviation_ratio.label: Spread ratio (xi)
deviation_ratio.description: How widely ants sample around an archived rule; acts as evaporation.

weight_decay.label: Ridge penalty on the weights
weight_decay.description: Subtracted from the training utility per unit of squared weight; larger keeps the rule simpler.

weight_bound.label: Weight bound
weight_bound.description: Every weight and the bias are searched inside [-bound, bound] (features are z-scores).

native.produces: The colony returns the single lowest-cost path or sequence that any ant built across all iterations, together with that path's total cost and the final pheromone levels on the edges.
native.targetVariable: the total cost of one complete path or ordering through the construction graph, for example the expected cost of a routing sequence across execution venues
native.objectiveNote: Natively the colony minimises the total cost of one path built step by step through a construction graph, with each ant choosing its next edge by pheromone strength and heuristic desirability and every deposit proportional to the inverse cost of the finished path; the Model Cycle replaces that routing cost with the tape utility of a position rule, which is recorded as the as-run objective.

metrics.why: The colony is an anytime search, so the lowest path cost it reports only means something beside the number of ants and iterations spent before pheromone reinforcement settled on that path.
metrics.baseline: the best path of the first iteration, built from the heuristic desirability alone before any pheromone was deposited

metrics.why: Pheromone memorises whatever paid on the costs the ants were shown, so the kept solution has to be scored again on later bars that neither the ants nor the stopping decision ever touched.
metrics.baseline: the same kept solution's objective on its own training span

metrics.why: Colony size times iterations is the count of paths scored, and every extra sampled path raises the chance that the single winner owes its cost to luck on the training data.
Each ant draws its next step at random, so two colonies started from different seeds can lay pheromone on different paths and the headline number needs its spread across those reruns.
Where held-out bars decide which iteration's best path is kept, the chosen figure is a maximum over iterations and flatters the colony, so it is displayed only next to the untouched test value.
metrics.baseline: the same kept solution's return on the fold's test tape

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: A pheromone-guided path search returns a routing or ordering, not a stream of trading returns, so this ratio grades the strategy that used the path and belongs to the as-run layer only.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: Alpha needs a benchmark-relative return series, and the colony's only native number is the cost of the best path it constructed.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: A drawdown needs an equity curve through time, while the colony's output is one static best path carrying a single cost.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The colony holds no portfolio and places no trades natively; turnover belongs to the trading rule the engine wraps around its answer.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: This ratio divides a yearly return by a drawdown, and neither quantity exists for a search whose whole result is a path cost.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: Conditional value at risk is a property of a return distribution, and the ants sample candidate paths rather than returns.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: The ants sample paths and never compute a bound on the best possible path, so no proven distance from the optimum exists to report.

asRun.standInNote: The specification describes ants walking a discrete construction graph of paths, while the runnable adapter uses the continuous-domain variant in which a ranked archive of weight vectors plays the pheromone and the ants sample new weights of one tanh-linear position rule around it; the as-run numbers therefore grade that linear rule and its validation-fitted probability curve, not a routing or sequencing answer.
asRun.probabilityNote: The kept rule's score, the weighted sum of the bar's features plus a bias, is passed through a two-parameter logistic curve whose slope and intercept are fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation rows.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the mean net utility per bar in move-scale units

meaningful.why: The ants were rewarded for net tape utility after one round trip of cost per decision, so net profit on the test walk is the closest out-of-sample reading of what the archive was searched for.

The archive's best weight vector gives a continuous score per bar, and this ranking number tests whether higher scores precede up moves while depending on the validation-fitted curve only through the sign of its slope.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training channel holds the lowest penalised energy seen on the training tape and the validation channel holds the unpenalised utility of another tape, so their difference is not an overfitting gap.
With no flat state the engine holds a position on every bar once the first call is made, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the annealed rule's own position size.

caveats: The curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the same validation rows whose tape utility chose which temperature level's rule was kept, so those rows were used twice.
If the validation rows give the curve a negative slope, the traded call is the opposite of the sign of the rule the chain was cooled toward.

The training energy sizes the position by the hyperbolic tangent of the score and charges a round trip of cost on every decision in proportion to that size, while the engine trades full size on the sign and charges cost only when the call flips, so the chain did not optimise the quantity the engine reports.
The reward tape is fixed: the market does not react to the rule and the rule's own position is not among its inputs.
Targets of neighbouring bars overlap by the label horizon, so intervals for these numbers need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract the costs are that contract's account figures applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

evolutionary_decision_rules.summary: Evolves readable if-then trading rules (feature above or below a threshold, joined by and / or / not); the best few rules vote on each bar.
evolutionary_decision_rules.implementationNote: Bridge: genetic programming (deap.gp, typed rule trees, vectorised over bars) evolves long-if-the-rule-fires rules against train-span net utility on the price tape; the best rules vote, the validation-best generation is kept, and P(up) is a logistic curve of the vote fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: thresholds on causal z-scored features only. Expect: readable rules, edge near the base rate.
evolutionary_decision_rules.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

epochs.label: Generations
epochs.description: How many generations the search runs (one engine epoch each).

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

tournament_size.label: Tournament size
tournament_size.description: Rules compared to pick each parent; larger is greedier.

crossover_probability.label: Crossover probability
crossover_probability.description: Chance a pair of parents swaps subtrees.

mutation_probability.label: Mutation probability
mutation_probability.description: Chance a child gets a new subtree or a redrawn threshold.

maximum_tree_depth.label: Maximum rule depth
maximum_tree_depth.description: Deepest nesting of conditions a rule may have.

ensemble_size.label: Rules in the vote
ensemble_size.description: How many of the best distinct rules vote on each bar.

parsimony_penalty.label: Penalty per node
parsimony_penalty.description: Subtracted from a rule's fitness for each node (bloat control).

native.produces: The fittest trading decision rule the population reached, either a parameter vector or a readable tree of indicator comparisons joined by logical operators, together with its fitness history across generations and its trade decisions on held-out bars.
native.targetVariable: The position the evolved rule takes on each bar (long, short or flat), chosen so that a backtest score of those positions over the training window is as high as the search could make it; it is a decision, not a forecast of the next move.
native.objectiveNote: The fitness is any scalar backtest score of the rule's simulated trades, so it needs no gradient, and genetic programming adds a charge per tree node so that a rule cannot buy fitness by growing until it memorises the training window.

metrics.why: Selection, crossover and mutation promise only that the fittest rule in the population gets better generation after generation, so the fitness of the best rule against the number of rules simulated so far is the direct record of whether the evolution was still climbing or had stalled.
metrics.baseline: The best fitness in the random first generation of the same run.

metrics.why: An evolved rule tree can fit the exact historical path it was bred on, so what its own long and short decisions earn after costs on bars that neither bred it nor chose the generation to stop at is the only honest reading of the fitness it was selected for.
metrics.baseline: Holding the same series long over the same test bars, which the specification names as the reference an evolved rule must beat.

metrics.why: Population size times generations is the number of rule trees whose backtest was looked at before one was kept, and the best of that many random-looking trees shows a good training fitness by luck alone.

The readable tree is the product of genetic programming, so the share of refits on other folds or seeds in which the same indicator comparisons reappear says whether the evolution found a rule or one accident of crossover.

The first generation, every tournament draw, every crossover point and every mutation come from the random seed, so two runs on the same bars evolve different trees and the spread of their held-out return shows how much of one result is the seed.

The specification stops the evolution at the generation whose validation-window fitness is highest, so that fitness is a maximum over generations and reads better than the same rule will on later bars.
metrics.baseline: The same rule's return on the test bars.

metrics.why: A tree of comparisons can evolve into a condition that is true on nearly every bar or on almost none, which is a constant position in disguise, so the share of bars on which the kept rule fires shows whether it makes a decision at all.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: Natively it could only be the fitness the population is bred on; as a result it belongs to the as-run layer, where it measures the engine's trading of the rule's call with costs.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark futures index or excess-return model appears anywhere in the specification, whose only reference is buy and hold on the same series.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: The specification lists drawdown as a possible non-differentiable fitness, not as a measure of the evolution; the traded drawdown is reported in the as-run layer.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: One evolved rule on one instrument has no portfolio weights to rebalance, so a turnover ratio of a portfolio never applied to it.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It needs a traded equity curve with costs, which exists only once the engine trades the rule's call, so it is an as-run number.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The evolved rule produces positions and not a loss distribution, and neither the specification nor the engine computes a conditional tail loss for it.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: Evolution offers no convergence guarantee and no bound on the best possible rule, so there is nothing to measure the returned rule's distance from.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: A rule that fires or does not fire states no probability, so natively there are no odds for a likelihood score to grade.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is the specification's genetic programming variant only: typed rule trees whose leaves compare one causal z-scored feature of the bar with a threshold, joined by both, either and negate, bred by tournament selection, one-point subtree crossover and subtree or threshold mutation. A rule is long when it fires and short when it does not and is never flat, its fitness is the net utility per bar on the training reward tape minus the penalty per node, a hall of fame keeps the best distinct rules and their vote is the score, the generation with the best validation tape utility is kept, and a logistic curve fitted on validation bars turns the vote into the probability of up, so the as-run numbers measure that vote plus that curve. The market does not react to the rule and its position is not part of its input.
asRun.probabilityNote: The score of a bar is twice the share of the hall-of-fame rules that fire on its feature row minus one, and the probability of up is a logistic curve of that score whose slope and intercept are fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars; the evolution maximised tape utility, so the vote has no probability meaning before the curve and takes only as many levels as there are rules in the vote plus one.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the mean net utility per decision bar in move-scale units; the training value is the single best rule ever seen with its penalty per node included, and the validation value is the whole vote with no penalty

meaningful.why: The rule trees were bred for money made on the training tape after costs, so the profit of the vote's call on the test walk is the closest out-of-sample reading of that fitness, on bars that neither the breeding nor the choice of generation touched.

A rule that fires on nearly every bar is a constant long position, so the profit over simply holding the same series is what shows that the evolved comparisons added anything beyond the drift of the training span.

The fitness rewarded mean utility per bar with no charge for variability, so the steadiness of the per-bar profit of the vote's call is a property the evolution was never asked for and is tested here for the first time.
The tape utility the trees were bred on has no drawdown term, so the deepest fall of the traded equity shows a risk that selection pressure never acted on.

It compares winning and losing trades that end when the vote's call flips, while each rule's fitness was paid per decision bar with a round trip charged on every bar, so the two count costs differently.
It counts trades closed in profit after costs, which depends on how long the vote keeps one side as much as on whether the evolved comparisons point the right way.

Threshold comparisons on z-scored features can flip the vote from bar to bar, and the fitness charged a full round trip on every bar whether or not the position changed, so the real flip rate shows how much cost the traded call actually pays.
It scores the cut of the curve at one half, which is the traded call and depends on the validation-fitted intercept and slope sign as well as on which rules fire.
It shows whether the vote's call finds both up bars and down bars or has settled on the side that paid on the training tape.
One symmetric number for the vote-plus-curve call, which sits near zero when the hall-of-fame rules amount to an always-long or always-short lean.

It grades the few probability levels the curve assigns to the possible vote shares, and being bounded it reads fairly even when the vote carries so little direction that every level sits close to one half.

It grades the stated odds of the vote after the validation-fitted curve; the generation was chosen on validation tape utility and not on this loss, so on test bars it is a fair second view of the vote-plus-curve.

It checks whether the up share observed at each vote level on test bars still matches the level the curve learned on validation bars; only a few bins are filled because the vote has only a few levels.
The curve is monotone, so the ordering of bars is the vote share itself, but with only as many levels as rules in the vote plus one the curve has a handful of points and most pairs of bars are ties.
It reports how many vote shares actually occurred in a fold, which is the number of points behind every ranking and calibration figure for this model.
It shows whether the hall-of-fame rules together call one side on nearly every bar, the sign that the evolution collapsed to the always or never condition.

The forecast comes from a second population of rule trees bred against the Huber loss of the scaled move, whose vote is multiplied by one least-squares scale, so this tests that second evolution against forecasting no move.
It is the miss in points of the separately evolved forecast, which can take only as many values as its vote has levels, read against the no-change error on the same bars.
It is the sign accuracy of the second, Huber-bred rule vote and so can disagree with the traded call, which comes from the utility-bred vote through the validation curve.

The training value logged each generation is the fitness of the best rule the hall of fame has ever held, so the curve by generation shows whether breeding was still finding better trees when the search stopped.
The fit summary counts every rule tree whose training utility was scored, and the larger that count the more of the kept rule's training fitness is the luck of the best of many.
The kept generation is the one whose vote earned the most on the validation tape, so that utility is a maximum over generations and is shown only beside the test value it flatters.

Population size, tournament size, crossover and mutation probabilities, tree depth, rules in the vote and the penalty per node are chosen by the traded Sharpe ratio on inner blocks of the training span, a selection score that is optimistic by construction.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training value is one rule's utility with its penalty per node and the validation value is the whole vote's utility with no penalty, so their difference compares two different quantities.
With long only off and no stop or target the engine is always in the market once the first call is made, so the share describes the engine's rule and not the evolved rules.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, so it is not a same-model reference for the vote-plus-curve probability.
A precision-recall curve over the handful of probability levels the vote can take is a few points joined by straight lines and adds nothing beyond the confusion counts.

caveats: The logistic curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the validation bars after the generation is chosen on those same bars, so the fitted slope can be negative and turn a rule bred as long when it fires into a short call, and only the test walk is out of sample.

Each rule's fitness charges one round trip of cost on every decision bar because a rule is always long or short, while the engine charges costs only when the traded call flips, so the training utility and the traded net profit are not the same arithmetic.

The moves on the reward tape are clipped in move-scale units before the fitness is computed, so one extreme training bar cannot decide which rule wins, and the tape utility is therefore not a plain sum of profit.

The thresholds are constants in z-score units on the causal feature row, not the indicator and price comparisons of the specification, and the always and never conditions are allowed, so a kept vote can be a constant position.
The vote can take only as many values as there are rules in the vote plus one, so the probability of up, the ranking metrics and the price forecast all move in a few steps.
The price forecast is a second, separately evolved population bred on the Huber loss of the scaled move and kept at its best validation Huber loss, so its sign need not match the traded call.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so any interval on these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For any root other than the micro Nasdaq contract the costs charged are that contract's account figures applied as a stated assumption, and the last bar of each fold exits at its close.

symbolic_regression.summary: Evolves a closed-form formula of the features (add, multiply, divide, log, ...) that predicts the coming move, and reads the direction from the formula's sign.
symbolic_regression.implementationNote: Bridge: gplearn genetic programming fits a formula to the train span's scaled h-bar move; the generation with the best validation error is kept and P(up) is a logistic curve of the formula's value fitted on validation (the formula is also the price forecast). Differs from the spec: moves clipped at 5 scale units. Expect: short formulas, weak edge; watch the printed formula.
symbolic_regression.estimatedTrainingTime: seconds to a few minutes per fold (paced replay adds its own time)

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: The search stops after this many epochs without a better validation score.

tournament_size.label: Tournament size
tournament_size.description: Formulas compared to pick each parent; larger is greedier.

crossover_probability.label: Crossover probability
crossover_probability.description: Share of children made by subtree crossover (the rest by mutation).
