parsimony_penalty.description: Added to a formula's error for each node (bloat control).

initial_tree_depth.label: Initial formula depth
initial_tree_depth.description: Deepest formula in the first generation.

native.produces: One human-readable closed-form formula of the input features, found by evolving a population of expression trees, which gives one number per bar as its forecast of the target, together with the formula's training fitness and node count.
native.targetVariable: The forward return of the instrument over the forecast horizon, as a signed size, explained as a formula of the features known at the bar's close.
native.objectiveNote: The fitness is the mean squared error of the candidate formula plus a parsimony penalty per node, and it is lowered by tournament selection, subtree crossover and mutation over generations instead of by a gradient, so the shape of the formula is searched as well as its constants.

metrics.why: The evolved formula is selected on squared misses, so on a later block its squared error is compared with forecasting no move at all, the persistence reference the specification demands every discovered formula beat.
metrics.baseline: The no-change forecast on the same resolved bars.

metrics.why: The product of the search is the expression tree itself, so a formula whose features and operators reappear when the evolution is rerun on another fold or seed is a finding, and one that is replaced by an unrelated tree each time was a fit to noise.
It states the kept formula's typical miss in price points on unseen bars, the same squared-miss quantity its fitness ranked the population by, in units a trader can set beside a stop distance.
metrics.baseline: The root mean square of the actual horizon moves on the same bars.

metrics.why: A short formula can have the right shape and the wrong scale, for example a saturating momentum term with too small a constant, and the correlation shows whether its larger outputs line up with larger realised moves regardless of that scale.

Population size times generations is the number of formulas scored on the same training bars, and the specification warns that a large enough search always finds an expression that fits noise, so the count is the multiple-testing exposure of the winner.

The kept formula's error on a later block minus its error on the bars it was evolved on shows how much of its fitness was bloat fitted to training noise, which is what the parsimony penalty and the depth cap exist to limit.

The best fitness in the population plotted against generations shows when the evolution stopped finding better expressions, which is the stopping signal the algorithm itself uses when fitness plateaus.

An evolved formula that contains a non-zero constant term forecasts a small move in one direction on every bar, and the mean signed miss exposes that lean, which would otherwise pass for skill during a trend.

notApplicable.name: Regime Log-Likelihood
notApplicable.why: It never applied: an evolved formula is a single-number forecast with no density and no hidden market states.

notApplicable.name: Regime Separation Index
notApplicable.why: It never applied: the formula forms no clusters, and the registry has no such metric.

notApplicable.name: fANOVA Variance Explained
notApplicable.why: It never applied as a model metric: it grades a hyperparameter search, while the formula is judged by its error on later bars.

notApplicable.name: SHAP Stability Score
notApplicable.why: It never applied: the expression is read directly, and whether it recurs across folds is measured by the structure stability metric instead.

notApplicable.name: Expected Calibration Error
notApplicable.why: It never applied natively: the formula's output is a forecast move with no probability attached to it.

notApplicable.name: Regime Persistence Ratio
notApplicable.why: It never applied: there is no Markov transition matrix because the formula has no states.

notApplicable.name: Brier score
notApplicable.why: Natively there is no probability of up to score; the probability the Model Cycle grades comes from a curve fitted on validation bars.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable adapter is genetic programming of an expression tree with tournament selection, crossover, mutation and a penalty per node as the specification describes, but its fitness is the mean absolute error instead of the mean squared error, its target is the horizon move divided by trailing volatility and clipped at a fixed bound, it has no saturating or trigonometric operators, the generation kept is the one with the lowest validation Huber loss, and the traded direction is a logistic curve of the formula's value fitted on validation bars, so the as-run direction numbers measure the formula plus that curve.
asRun.probabilityNote: The kept generation's best formula is evaluated on the bar's feature row and the probability of up is an unweighted logistic curve of that value, with slope and intercept fitted on the fold's validation bars against the up or down labels.

stepQuantity.unit: mean absolute difference between the generation's best formula and the scaled horizon move, in move-scale units

meaningful.why: The price formula is evolved on absolute misses, so its absolute error on test bars against forecasting no move is the matching test of whether the evolved expression learned anything about the size and sign of the move.

The direction formula's value is continuous and the validation curve only rescales it, so this asks directly whether bars where the evolved expression is higher went up more often than bars where it is lower.
It shows what trading the side given by the direction formula's curve earned after costs, which is the practical test of an expression that was fitted to move size and never to profit.
A formula with a constant term can lean to one side on every bar, and the profit beyond holding the contract separates what its feature terms add from that lean.
It relates the per-bar profit of trading the formula's call to its variability, read with the predicted up share because a short formula often holds one side for long stretches.
It shows the deepest equity fall while following the formula's call, which is large when the expression's sign stays wrong through a sustained move.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost on the trades opened each time the formula's curve-mapped value crossed one half, after costs.
It is the share of winning trades among the flips of the formula's call and must be read with the trade count, since a smooth formula flips rarely.
It grades the odds produced by passing the formula's value through the validation curve, so it tests the formula and the curve together, read against quoting the fold's training up share.
It grades the same curve-mapped formula value with a bounded score, so one bar where a division or logarithm in the expression produced an extreme value cannot dominate it.
The curve is unweighted so its odds can be compared with observed up shares, though a weak formula keeps the probabilities near the base rate and fills only a couple of bins.

A slope below one on test bars means the validation curve trusted the formula's value more than the later bars justify, the usual result when the generation and the curve were chosen on the same validation bars.
It counts how often the side of the curve-mapped formula value matched the move, read against the majority class because the curve's intercept carries the validation base rate.
It averages the up recall and the down recall, so a formula that calls one side almost always scores one half whatever the mix of up and down bars.
It sums the four cells of the formula's hard calls into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the expression has no directional content.
It is the price formula's own fitness quantity carried to test bars and converted to points, to be read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same bars.
It tests the sign of the price formula alone, with no validation curve in between, on the bars where its tick-rounded forecast is not zero.
It shows whether larger outputs of the price formula go with larger realised moves even when the formula's scale is too small to beat the no-change forecast.
A constant term in the evolved expression shifts every forecast the same way, and the mean signed miss shows that shift.

The forecast line comes from a second formula evolved separately from the one behind the traded call, so the share of bars where the two point the same way shows how far the picture and the trade can disagree.

Training and validation loss are both the mean absolute error of the generation's best formula against the scaled move, so their gap for the kept generation shows how much of the fitness was fitted to training noise.
The training loss logged at each generation is the best formula's absolute error so far, so its curve shows when the evolution stopped improving.
Population size times the generations run is the number of expressions scored on the training bars, the multiple-testing exposure of the formula that was kept.
The search over population size, tournament size, crossover probability and penalty per node is scored by the shared tuning objective, an optimistic selection score read beside the fold's test value.
It shows whether the formula's curve-mapped value ever crosses one half or simply sits on the side of the validation base rate.
It counts how often the formula's call changed side, which sets how much weight the trade-based ratios can bear.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: With long-only off and no stop or target the engine is always in the market once the first call is made, so the share describes the engine's rule and not the formula.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, so it is not a same-series reference the formula could have used.

caveats: The registry note says the formula is also the price forecast, but the engine fits the price model as a separate evolution on the unclipped scaled move, so the forecast line and the traded call come from two different formulas.
The validation bars choose which generation is kept and then fit the logistic curve's slope and intercept, so both the formula and its probability scale have seen those bars.
The direction formula is fitted to scaled moves clipped at a fixed bound, so very large moves count no more than moves at the bound.
On a bar where any feature is missing or the expression returns a non-finite value the model makes no prediction and the engine holds the existing position.

The kept generation is selected on the validation Huber loss while the loss charted for validation is the mean absolute error, so the starred epoch is not always the lowest point of the charted curve.
Forecasts are rounded to the tick before scoring, so a formula whose outputs are smaller than half a tick is scored as forecasting no move.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so intervals need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For roots other than MNQ the cost per side is the MNQ account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
